messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Problems with stepsize adaptation?
parts:
Hello,

I have problems with divergent iterations in a
negative binomial regression model.
As far as i can tell I have used the suggested
means to re-parameterize the model (non-centered
parameterization).

Now I am wondering if there is maybe a problem with
the adaptation of the stepsize.
When I look at the adaptation of the stepsize
in the terminal buffer, I observe that the stepsize
does not decrease, even though the acceptance
rate consistently falls below the threshold I 
specified (see figure, the attached pdf includes some
basic diagnostic plots).


(The circle size in the bottom right panel indicates the number of 
iterations for each stepsize bin.)

Is this expected behavior, or is there something 
I can do to insure that the stepsize decreases in
the terminal buffer?


Guido


Some additional notes:
- It does not seem to matte a lot if I set adapt_delta 
  to .95 or .99.
- non centered parameterization helps to get all
  entries of the mass matrix to around 1, with exceptions
  of the values in the cholesky factor of the correlation
  matrix, which are 1-2 orders of magnitude smaller.
-  It might also be interesting that
  the same model works fine as a hierarchical model 
  (but I need this model to compare it o the hierarchical
   model). 
- This model is ease to fit if I sample the regression 
  parameter independently. The problems began when I
  started using a multivariate normal.



######## relevant model sections ################

data {
  ...
  vector[K] sdbeta;
  vector[K] sdalpha;
  vector[K] mbeta;
  vector[K] malpha;
}

parameters {
   cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega; 
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;    
  vector[K] gamma;                          
  vector[K] beta;
  vector[K] alpha;              
  real<lower=0> raw_phi;
}

transformed parameters {
  real phi;
  vector[K] tmp;
  vector[K] scaled_beta;
  vector[K] scaled_alpha;
  
  // not sure if the following is OK
  // but the over-dispersion parameter 
  // is hard to sample from if one uses the 
  // cauchy or its non-centered parameterization
  phi <- 6 + inv_logit(raw_phi)*1.5; 

  scaled_beta <- mbeta + beta .* sdbeta;
  scaled_alpha <- malpha + alpha .* sdalpha;
}

model {
  vector[N_train] thetas;
  vector[N_train] etas;
  matrix[K, K] Sigma_beta;

  raw_phi ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  tau ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
  gamma ~ normal(0,2); # orig scale = 5
  alpha[K] ~ normal(0,5); # orig scale = 5
  alpha[1:(K-1)] ~ normal(0,2); # orig scale = 5
  
  Sigma_beta <- quad_form_diag(L_Omega * L_Omega', tau);
  beta ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma_beta);
  
  thetas <- to_vector(sx * scaled_alpha);
  etas <- to_vector(sx * scaled_beta);

...
}

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Problems with stepsize adaptation?
parts:
On Thursday, August 25, 2016 at 10:12:48 AM UTC-4, Guido Biele wrote:
I have problems with divergent iterations in a
negative binomial regression model.
Negative binomial models are difficult, and there could be many culprits. One general thing pertains to these lines

Sigma_beta <- quad_form_diag(L_Omega * L_Omega', tau);
  beta ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma_beta);

By constructing Sigma_beta and passing that to multi_normal (which takes its Cholesky factorization) you can lose a good bit of numerical accuracy. Just pass tau * L_Omega to multi_normal_cholesky() like

target += multi_normal_cholesky_lpdf(beta | gamma, tau * L_Omega);

However, that does not address problems due to differing scales among correlated betas. It is often but not always better to use the stochastic representation of the multivariate normal so that

beta = gamma + tau * (L_Omega * z); // implies: beta ~ multi_normal_cholesky(gamma, tau * L_Omega)

is a transformed parameter, z is a parameter vector, and in the model block

target += normal_lpdf(z | 0, 1);

From Stan's perspective, working in z-space is frequently easier than working in beta-space.

Ben

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Re: Problems with stepsize adaptation?
parts:
Thanks for the feedback Ben!

I had tried the full non-centered parameterization before,
but this (a)

parameters {
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;

matrix[K,1] gamma;                          
  matrix[K,1] z;
  vector[K] alpha;
  ...
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[K,1] beta;
  ...
  beta <- gamma +  diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega) * z;

}

model {
  vector[N_train] thetas;
  vector[N_train] etas;

to_vector(tau) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
  to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0,2);
  alpha[K] ~ normal(0,5);
alpha[1:(K-1)] ~ normal(0,2);

...
}


is clearly slower then this (b)

parameters {
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;      
  vector[K] gamma;                          
  vector[K] beta;
  vector[K] alpha;                
}

transformed parameters {
 ...

}

model {
  vector[N_train] thetas;
  vector[N_train] etas;
  matrix[K, K] Sigma_beta;

tau ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
  gamma ~ normal(0,2);

alpha[K] ~ normal(0,5);
  alpha[1:(K-1)] ~ normal(0,2);
  Sigma_beta <- quad_form_diag(L_Omega * L_Omega', tau);
  beta ~ multi_normal(gamma, Sigma_beta);
  ...
}

I think the reason for the difference in speed is that
the step-size for model (b) is an order of magnitude larger 
than for (a). 

Still, model (a) with the full non-centered parameterization
of the multivariate gaussian seems indeed a bit more stable,
because I don't need to use target acceptance rates as high as
.99 to reduce the number of divergent iterations. But even here 
a few divergent iterations remain.

Could it be that the root of my problems is that in models (a) 
and (b) the diagonal of the inverse of the mass matrix for 
L_Omega is generally smaller (median of 0.04) than for the
other parameters (median of 1.5). Is there a way to scale 
L_Omega such that the diagonal of the inverse of the mass
matrix becomes larger for the L_Omega parameters?

Best - Guido
